bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: From the horizon to a distant observer
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
In Lesson 15, light inside the horizon could not escape. Here we use the same Schwarzschild geometry and place a quantum field on it. After collapse, an initially empty state can give an outgoing flux of quanta when analyzed in terms of late-time modes far away.

$$r_s=2GM/c^2$$

+++ A closer look
Select a solar mass. The radius in the readout is the physical value, about 2.95 km. The rim in the drawing is logarithmically compressed to fit very different masses on one screen. The dots depict the exterior flux. Do not infer a physical frequency from the spacing between two dots. The temperature and spectrum in the readout are the quantities associated with a distant measurement.
+++

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] The familiar story: «right at the horizon the vacuum keeps creating pairs of virtual particles; one falls in, the other flies out». Hawking himself used this picture to make the result easy to imagine, but the actual calculation follows no trajectory of any pair. It compares how the quantum field splits into modes before the hole forms and long afterwards. Switch on the particle-pair picture to see that story; do not read it as real motion.

> [Thử ngay] [[Select a solar mass|thu]] [[Toggle the particle-pair picture|cap]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
A stationary, uncharged, nonrotating hole has a {{nhiệt độ Hawking|Hawking temperature}} set by mass alone. This is the temperature inferred from the spectrum far from the hole. An observer close by in a strong gravitational field uses a different local clock and energy calibration.

$$T_H=\hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$$

+++ A closer look
In the formula ħ enters through quantum physics, G through gravity and k_B converts energy to temperature. Double M and watch the radius grow as the temperature falls. A higher pitch illustrates a higher temperature using an audible mapping. Comparing at the same location separates the effect of changing mass from that of changing the observer's position. Keep the distant-observer convention throughout the lesson.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Double M|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: One scale for many orders of magnitude
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Dragging the mass knob right scales its value in powers of ten. Radius is proportional to M and temperature to its inverse, so their product stays fixed. This lets you compare the two measurements without knowing the mass in advance.

$$T_H r_s=\hbar c/(4\pi k_B)$$

+++ A closer look
A hypothetical hole of 10¹² kg is at about 1.23 × 10¹¹ K. This high temperature goes with a very small horizon radius. The model varies a parameter. It does not simulate a single real object being compressed from one mass to another. Increase the mass and predict whether the temperature will be higher or lower before reading it. Use the actual mass values for each setting in your reasoning.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare with a 10¹² kg hole|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the mass close to 10²² kg, to within about 8%.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: Watch the exponent on the scale.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Each blue bar represents radiated power in a narrow frequency interval. The coordinate x is photon energy divided by k_B T. In terms of x, one curve describes the ideal blackbody shape at all temperatures.

$$x=h\nu/(k_BT),\qquad B_\nu\propto x^3/(e^x-1)$$

+++ A closer look
The frequency peak is at x ≈ 2.821. When mass decreases the peak frequency rises while its dimensionless coordinate stays put. In spectral power per unit wavelength the bin width changes along with the axis, giving a different peak. The probe highlights one point on the curve. Move across both sides of the peak rather than just choosing the tallest bar.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Place the probe at the peak|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the probe to the peak, within 0.075 in x.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: Try near x = 2.8 and compare the heights on either side.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Take the horizon area and assign it the photon emission of an ideal blackbody. Its area times σT⁴ gives the power in the readout. This deliberate estimate makes the mass dependence easy to follow.

$$P_{\rm id}=4\pi r_s^2\sigma T_H^4\propto M^{-2}$$

+++ A closer look
Doubling M quadruples the area but reduces T⁴ by a factor of sixteen. The power falls to one quarter. In the field calculation the surrounding scattering potential gives frequency- and spin-dependent transmission factors, known as greybody factors. This is why the power readout is labeled ideal. An actual emission calculation must also identify which particle fields can be excited at that temperature.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare power after doubling M|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Select an ideal 2.725 K bath, close to today’s cosmic microwave background temperature. The hole both absorbs incoming photons and emits photons. The direction of net exchange depends on which side is hotter. Equal temperatures balance the two flows in this model. The balancing mass is about 4.5 × 10²² kg, roughly six tenths of the Moon's mass, yet its horizon is only about 0.07 mm across.

$$T_H(M_{\rm eq})=T_{\rm bath}$$

+++ A closer look
A solar-mass hole is much colder than this bath. It still has a Hawking temperature even as net energy flows in. To test balance here, keep the bath on and vary M until the temperatures agree. This balance is unstable. If the hole gains a little mass it cools, absorbs more than it emits, grows and cools further. If it loses a little it heats up, emits more than it absorbs, shrinks and heats further. The reason is that a black hole has negative heat capacity: losing energy makes it hotter, the opposite of an ordinary body.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Toggle the photon bath|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Keep the bath on and drag M until T_H differs from 2.725 K by less than 9%.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Put the hole in vacuum and use the ideal power from the previous step. Lost energy equals lost mass times c². Power grows as M decreases, so dividing initial energy by initial power gives a time three times too long.

$$\frac{dM}{dt}=-\frac{P_{\rm id}}{c^2},\qquad t_{\rm id}=\frac{5120\pi G^2M_0^3}{\hbar c^4}$$

> [Ví dụ] A solar-mass hole radiates an ideal photon power of only about 9 × 10⁻²⁹ W and needs about 2 × 10⁶⁷ years to evaporate completely, more than 10⁵⁷ times the age of the universe (1.38 × 10¹⁰ years). By the same formula only a hole of about 1.7 × 10¹¹ kg evaporates completely within 13.8 billion years. Including all particle species and greybody factors, detailed calculations give about 5 × 10¹¹ kg (Carr et al., 2010).

+++ A closer look
Integrating M² dM from the starting mass down to zero gives the cubic scaling. Double the mass and the ideal lifetime increases eightfold. Extrapolation all the way to zero goes beyond the reliable semiclassical regime. Interpret the result under its assumptions. A real hole may absorb gas or radiation, rotate, or emit other particle species. Each can change the evolution.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare lifetimes at twice the mass|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
The temperature calculation quantizes matter fields on a classical geometry. Slow evaporation can be approximated by a succession of holes of slightly different mass. This is reasonable while a typical quantum carries little energy compared with the hole’s total energy.

$$k_BT_H/(Mc^2)=\hbar c/(8\pi G M^2)$$

+++ A closer look
Near the Planck mass, changes in the geometry and quantum gravity become essential. The dots illustrate statistical emission. The lifetime formula cannot decide the final fate of the hole. As you vary mass, ask which quantities follow from the Hawking temperature and which require the extra perfect-blackbody assumption. The distinction determines how precisely to interpret the power and lifetime columns.
+++

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.ten: Hawking temperature of a Schwarzschild hole
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: Temperature assigned to the spectrum measured far away.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: Photon-only model using the horizon area.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: Integrate the ideal blackbody photon power to M = 0, neglecting external absorption.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: In the same vacuum conditions, halve the mass. How does T change?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: Temperature is inversely proportional to mass.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: The hole is colder than the surrounding photon bath. Which way is the net energy flow?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: In an ideal uniform bath, absorption exceeds emission when the bath is hotter.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: The mass doubles. What fraction of the initial power remains in the blackbody model?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: Area and T⁴ together make power inversely proportional to M².
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does the peak stay fixed on the x axis as the temperature rises?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: The physical peak frequency is fixed
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: x divides the photon energy by k_B T
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: A fixed peak x corresponds to a physical peak frequency proportional to temperature.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: The model extrapolates M to zero. Why does that not determine the final state?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.dap: At very small masses a quantum’s energy stops being a small perturbation and prescribed classical geometry ceases to be reliable. The final regime calls for a quantum description of gravity.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Characteristic temperature of black-hole quantum radiation for a distant observer.
bai.moTa: Vary the mass, read the temperature, probe the spectrum and compare the hole with its surroundings.
bai.yChinh: A quantum field on the spacetime of a black hole formed by collapse produces an outgoing radiation flux far away. A lighter Schwarzschild hole has a higher Hawking temperature.
bai.giaiThich: The black sphere marks the horizon of an uncharged, nonrotating hole. Colored points outside it illustrate the flux. The graph shows the ideal blackbody frequency spectrum on a dimensionless horizontal axis. Sizes and timing are rescaled for visibility.
bai.conSo.1: A solar-mass hole has a temperature of about 6.17 × 10⁻⁸ K.
bai.conSo.2: In a 2.725 K photon bath the mass at the same temperature is about 4.5 × 10²² kg.
bai.hieuDung: A virtual-pair cartoon does not give particle trajectories in Hawking’s calculation. The calculation uses field modes in curved spacetime. Marks outside the horizon only illustrate the predicted energy flux.
bai.nguon: Written by Trí Lữ. S. W. Hawking, Particle Creation by Black Holes, Communications in Mathematical Physics 43 (1975), 199–220. B. J. Carr, K. Kohri, Y. Sendouda and J. Yokoyama, Physical Review D 81 (2010), 104019. NIST, 2022 CODATA constants.

canh.tt-chan-troi: The radius is compressed logarithmically. Gold dots are outgoing radiation; their rate on screen only grows with the order of magnitude of the power, not in true proportion.
canh.tt-pho: Horizontal axis x = hν/(k_B T_H). Blue bars are the black-hole spectrum, the gold line the photon-bath spectrum on the same scale; the hole's highest bar is 1 unless the bath dominates.
